cards.scenario: Mobile game, custom IdP not SAML or OIDC, easy free-to-premium transition, LEAST development effort.
cards.ok: One Cognito identity pool with a developer-authenticated provider calling the custom IdP, plus two authentication flows in the app.
cards.bad: Two Cognito identity pools, one per tier, each with its own authentication flow for free and premium users.
cards.why: A single identity pool makes tier transition easy; two pools double the work and require moving users between pools.

cards.scenario: Cross-account assume role fails for Auditor; only Auditor in AccountB may assume EC2Audit.
cards.ok: In AccountA, add a trust policy to EC2Audit naming arn:aws:iam::AccountB:user/Auditor.
cards.bad: In AccountA, add a trust policy to EC2Audit naming arn:aws:iam::AccountB:user/* for all users.
cards.why: Wildcard trust lets every AccountB user assume the role; only the specific Auditor ARN meets the requirement.

cards.scenario: SCP1 denies root, SCP2 denies non-us-west-2; Dev only us-west-2, Prod any Region; LEAST overhead.
cards.ok: Attach SCP1 to the organization root and attach SCP2 to the Dev OU.
cards.bad: Attach SCP1 to all accounts individually and attach SCP2 to each Dev account individually.
cards.why: SCPs inherit down the tree; attaching at root and OU level enforces the rules for existing and future accounts without per-account work.

cards.scenario: Operators in multiple accounts lose S3 access at once after centralizing security policies.
cards.ok: Sign in to the management account as an IAM user, open Organizations, and correct the SCP blocking S3.
cards.bad: Sign in to each member account as root, open Organizations, and correct the SCP blocking S3.
cards.why: Simultaneous failures point to an SCP; member accounts cannot view or change SCPs, and the management account is unaffected by them.

cards.scenario: Deploy AWS Config rules to almost all accounts plus management account, exclude a few, prevent unauthorized changes.
cards.ok: Activate trusted access with a delegated administrator, and deploy an AWS Config organization conformance pack with an exclusion list.
cards.bad: Deploy the template with CloudFormation StackSets across accounts and run drift detection frequently to ensure consistency.
cards.why: Drift detection only detects changes and does not prevent them; organization conformance packs are modifiable only by the delegated administrator.

cards.scenario: WorkSpaces with on-premises AD over Direct Connect; credentials not stored outside company; SSO.
cards.ok: Create an AD Connector in the WorkSpaces VPC using an on-premises service account, and use it as the WorkSpaces directory.
cards.bad: Create an AD Connector deployed on premises using a service account, and use it as the WorkSpaces directory.
cards.why: AD Connector is a directory gateway that caches nothing in the cloud, but it cannot be deployed on premises.

cards.scenario: Retiring on-premises AD; hundreds of users, basic LDAP, MFA required; LEAST operational effort.
cards.ok: Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD and migrate on-premises users with Active Directory Migration Toolkit.
cards.bad: Create Simple Active Directory and migrate users with the CSVDE utility.
cards.why: Simple AD does not support MFA; AD Connector depends on on-premises AD that is being retired.

cards.scenario: Design account structure for 500 workloads: environments, security team, a few unique workloads with special SCPs.
cards.ok: OUs per environment with SCPs, separate security accounts for logging, tooling and audit, and an Exceptions OU for unique workloads.
cards.bad: One centralized security account for all logging, tooling and audit; exception accounts left in regular OUs with account-level SCPs.
cards.why: Security functions belong in separate accounts for isolation; a separate Exceptions OU avoids complicated per-account SCP management.

cards.scenario: Find external principals with access to an SQS queue shared across the organization and outside accounts.
cards.ok: IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as zone of trust; filter external findings on the SQS queue.
cards.bad: IAM Access Analyzer with the current account as zone of trust; filter external findings on the SQS queue.
cards.why: Account zone of trust also flags other internal accounts; organization zone of trust reports only truly external principals.

cards.scenario: Share common SCPs between HR and Recruiting OUs, where Recruiting has extra restrictions; LEAST effort.
cards.ok: Rename Recruiting, create new Recruiting as child OU under HR, move accounts, trim duplicate rules from its SCP.
cards.bad: Move Recruiting accounts out of the organization, recreate Recruiting under HR, re-add accounts, trim SCP.
cards.why: Moving accounts out requires new invitations to return; make the more restricted OU the child so it inherits HR SCP.

cards.scenario: Standardize tags across Organizations accounts, correct noncompliant tags, then enforce compliant tags.
cards.ok: Tag policies, Resource Groups to find noncompliance, fix via the owning service, and SCPs to enforce tags.
cards.bad: Tag policies with prevent noncompliant operations option, plus Resource Groups to find and correct tags.
cards.why: Tag policy enforcement does not affect resources created with no tags; an SCP is required to enforce tag presence.

cards.scenario: Two-AZ VPC design with one NAT gateway, ALB, ASG, DynamoDB; increase resilience.
cards.ok: Create a second NAT gateway in the other Availability Zone and update the private subnet route tables.
cards.bad: Create DynamoDB global tables with replicas in two different AWS Regions for resilience.
cards.why: A NAT gateway is highly available only within its own AZ; ALB, internet gateway, and DynamoDB already span AZs by default.

cards.scenario: Two transit gateways in one Region; now all 10 VPCs must communicate fully.
cards.ok: Remove VPC-7 to VPC-10 attachments from TGW-B, attach them to TGW-A, add static routes, and delete TGW-B.
cards.bad: Create a transit gateway in another Region, attach VPC-7 to VPC-10, and peer it with TGW-A.
cards.why: VPCs must be in the same Region as the transit gateway; attachments must be removed from TGW-B before it can be deleted.

cards.scenario: Flow logs: A to B request ACCEPT, B reply from port 5001 to 20641 REJECT; fix it.
cards.ok: Modify the network ACL in Instance B subnet to allow outbound traffic on ephemeral port 20641.
cards.bad: Modify the security group inbound rules on the ENI to allow port 20641 for return traffic.
cards.why: Security groups are stateful and auto-allow return traffic, so a rejected reply means the stateless network ACL blocks it.

cards.scenario: Transit gateway shared via RAM; production and development VPCs must be fully isolated from each other.
cards.ok: Separate TGW route tables for production and development; remove default association and propagation; associate each VPC attachment accordingly.
cards.bad: Tag VPC attachments and edit the TGW route table to route tagged attachments to each other.
cards.why: TGW route tables route by CIDR, not tags; separate route tables act like VRFs for isolation.

cards.scenario: On-premises plus multiple VPCs with VGWs; scalable connectivity; LEAST operational overhead; add VPCs later.
cards.ok: Transit gateway with a Site-to-Site VPN attachment and VPC attachments; remove the virtual private gateways.
cards.bad: Transit VPC with VPN connections from the transit VPC to each virtual private gateway and to the customer gateway.
cards.why: A transit VPC requires managing EC2 router instances; transit gateway has nothing to manage.

cards.scenario: Static site, device-specific resources, high EC2 load, global users. Improve response times.
cards.ok: Move content to S3, serve through CloudFront, and use Lambda@Edge to load different resources based on the User-Agent header.
cards.bad: Move content to S3, serve through CloudFront, and use the User-Agent header itself to load different content.
cards.why: Lambda@Edge serves device-specific content with edge caching; forwarding raw User-Agent has many values and sends more requests to the origin.

cards.scenario: Apex domain, two Regions, highly available, faster for global users, ALB endpoints.
cards.ok: Public hosted zone with latency-based alias records for the apex domain, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes.
cards.bad: Public hosted zone with latency-based CNAME records for the apex domain, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes.
cards.why: A CNAME cannot be mapped to an apex domain, so alias records are required; private zones do not serve internet traffic.

cards.scenario: Multi-Region microservices; reroute traffic on full or partial failure using multiple CloudWatch metrics.
cards.ok: Route 53 ARC routing controls and health checks, with Lambda functions invoked by metric alarms toggling the routing controls.
cards.bad: Route 53 ARC readiness checks, with Lambda functions invoked from the readiness checks updating Route 53 record sets.
cards.why: Readiness checks only assess recovery capacity and do not route traffic; routing controls are on/off switches that can be automated from alarms.

cards.scenario: Make S3 static and ECS/ALB dynamic content reachable through CloudFront only.
cards.ok: CloudFront adds a custom origin header, an ALB-associated WAF web ACL validates it, and an OAC restricts S3 to CloudFront.
cards.bad: Have the ALB add the custom header and attach the WAF web ACL that validates it to the CloudFront distribution.
cards.why: CloudFront adds the header and ALBs do not create headers; a web ACL on CloudFront would block all traffic, so the ACL belongs on the ALB.

cards.scenario: Active-active two Regions, two static IP addresses for customers, LOWEST latency.
cards.ok: NLBs in each Region with AWS Global Accelerator pointing to both NLBs.
cards.bad: ALBs in each Region with a Route 53 latency routing record pointing to both ALBs.
cards.why: Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs and uses the AWS global network; ALBs do not support static IP addresses.

cards.scenario: CloudFront with two S3 origins; first bucket open to CloudFront and other AWS resources, second CloudFront only.
cards.ok: Create an OAC per bucket; bucket policies: first allows other AWS resources and the OAC, second allows only the OAC.
cards.bad: Write bucket policies naming the CloudFront distribution as principal and other AWS resources, without using an OAC.
cards.why: A distribution cannot be a principal in a bucket policy; the OAC represents CloudFront as a principal in the resource policy.

cards.scenario: A/B test two S3 sites via CloudFront; Europe to new design, US to current, with per-user exceptions.
cards.ok: Single CloudFront distribution with Lambda@Edge routing requests to different origins based on request attributes.
cards.bad: Single CloudFront distribution with a path-based behavior per version and Lambda@Edge on the default path to redirect clients.
cards.why: Lambda@Edge attaches to a distribution, not a path, and redirects reveal the versions to users; origin selection by attributes keeps the test hidden.

cards.scenario: Multiplayer game with heavy UDP traffic expanding beyond Europe; LOWEST latency for users.
cards.ok: Environments in multiple Regions with an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator and endpoints from each Region.
cards.bad: Environments in multiple Regions with Route 53 latency-based routing.
cards.why: Global Accelerator routes over the AWS global network and supports UDP; Route 53 latency routing uses the public internet.

cards.scenario: Developers self-create resources; limit them to two approved standard configurations.
cards.ok: Create Service Catalog products for dev and test, attach an IAM role to the products, and let developers launch the products.
cards.bad: Store CloudFormation templates for each configuration in S3 and grant IAM policies to create stacks from them.
cards.why: Service Catalog products use a launch role, so developers need no direct privileges; with CloudFormation they would need direct permissions and are not limited.

cards.scenario: Unexpected peak sales slow the site; EC2 CPU metrics do not correlate with peaks.
cards.ok: Dynamic scaling target tracking policy on the ALB request count per target metric.
cards.bad: Dynamic scaling target tracking policy on average CPU utilization of the Auto Scaling group.
cards.why: Peaks do not correlate with EC2 metrics such as CPU, but request count per target reflects load; scheduled and predictive scaling need predictable timing.

cards.scenario: Tightly coupled HPC cluster on Linux EC2; increase network throughput and reduce latency.
cards.ok: Use an EFA-capable instance type, run the cluster in a single Availability Zone, and disable CPU hyperthreading.
cards.bad: Use burstable instances, deploy in a partition placement group, and use a paravirtual (PV) AMI.
cards.why: EFA and single-AZ give low-latency node traffic; partition groups spread instances and raise latency, and PV AMIs cannot use enhanced networking.

cards.scenario: Migrate CMS from runbook to AWS; LEAST operational overhead, easy future changes.
cards.ok: CloudFormation template creating the VPC, EC2, and RDS, with EC2 user data to install and configure the software.
cards.bad: CloudFormation template creating the VPC, EC2, and RDS, then update the runbook for the remaining software steps.
cards.why: User data automates the software install too, and stack updates handle future changes; the runbook leaves installation manual.

cards.scenario: Migrate independent Linux apps with MySQL; remove Linux administration; minimal redesign; LEAST operational effort.
cards.ok: Containerize the apps on ECS with the Fargate launch type and migrate the databases to RDS for MySQL.
cards.bad: Containerize the apps on ECS with the EC2 launch type and migrate the databases to RDS for MySQL.
cards.why: The EC2 launch type still requires operating system management; Fargate removes the hosts and the Linux administration.

cards.scenario: Migrate Java order processing with Oracle DB; no servers to manage; keep Oracle expertise.
cards.ok: SQS holds orders, Lambda processes them, Amazon RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ keeps the backend database.
cards.bad: SQS holds orders, Lambda processes them, and the backend database is converted to Amazon Aurora.
cards.why: Converting Oracle to Aurora or DynamoDB discards the Oracle expertise; EC2 would mean managing servers.

cards.scenario: Five EC2 instances with slow boot, idle up to a month; need quick stop and start.
cards.ok: Encrypt root snapshot, create new AMI, launch new instances with hibernation enabled, and hibernate when idle.
cards.bad: Encrypt root snapshot, attach new root volume to existing instances and enable hibernation in instance options.
cards.why: Hibernation must be enabled at launch with an encrypted root volume, so existing instances cannot be modified.

cards.scenario: ALB and EC2 spike 2 to 10 times in minutes; Auto Scaling must react to repeated changes fastest.
cards.ok: Step scaling policy based on the CPUUtilization metric.
cards.bad: Step scaling policy based on the RequestCountPerTarget metric from the ALB.
cards.why: Step scaling responds during an ongoing scale-out; requests vary in cost, so CPU reflects load better than request count.

cards.scenario: Replatform three-tier app (server-side JavaScript, Python, MySQL) with least development; highly available, low overhead.
cards.ok: Containerize UI and logic on ECS Fargate behind ALB, with RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ.
cards.bad: Static UI on S3 and CloudFront, logic converted to Lambda with API Gateway, Aurora MySQL.
cards.why: Lambda conversion is re-architecting; server-side JavaScript UI cannot run as an S3 static website.

cards.scenario: Share AMI IDs for test EC2 across accounts and three Regions; LEAST operational overhead for each new AMI.
cards.ok: CloudFormation template with a Mappings section of AMI IDs per Region, deployed through one StackSet to all accounts.
cards.bad: Template with a Mappings section of AMI IDs, imported and run separately in each account.
cards.why: StackSets deploy one template across accounts and Regions; per-account copies of templates add maintenance. Templates only create resources in their own account.

cards.scenario: Restartable monthly AWS Batch job needs a custom AMI; cut management overhead and cost.
cards.ok: Managed EC2 compute environment using the custom AMI with the Spot provisioning model.
cards.bad: Fargate compute environment with the Fargate Spot provisioning model.
cards.why: Custom AMI requires an EC2 compute environment; Fargate does not support custom AMIs. Spot suits restartable monthly work.

cards.scenario: Grid computing on EC2 has network timeouts; adding instances from AMI did not help; LEAST operational effort.
cards.ok: Launch instances from the existing AMI in a cluster placement group and terminate the old ones.
cards.bad: Configure Elastic Network Adapters for all the instances.
cards.why: Cluster placement group lowers inter-instance latency with the AMI ready; ENA or EFA configuration takes significant effort.

cards.scenario: Conference registration PHP LAMP app, developer lacks AWS expertise; predictable pricing; LEAST time learning.
cards.ok: Amazon Lightsail instance from a preconfigured template with Lightsail object storage for static files.
cards.bad: Package app as a zip on Elastic Beanstalk with DynamoDB for data and S3 for static files.
cards.why: Beanstalk pricing follows resource consumption, not predictable; DynamoDB needs learning. Lightsail has flat monthly plans and a LAMP template.

cards.scenario: Replace call center: receive calls, contact flows, recognize caller intent, query business applications.
cards.ok: Amazon Connect for the contact center, Amazon Lex for intent recognition, and AWS Lambda to query internal business systems.
cards.bad: Amazon Rekognition to identify callers, Alexa for Business for conversational interfaces, and SQS to queue incoming callers.
cards.why: Connect builds contact flows, Lex gives ASR and NLU intent, Lambda integrates with Lex; Rekognition is images, Alexa is devices, Connect already queues.

cards.scenario: Two added Memcached nodes sit idle; fix with LEAST code changes.
cards.ok: Discover the new node endpoints with the AWS CLI and configure the application to read and write to all endpoints.
cards.bad: Replace Memcached with Redis, cluster mode disabled, and add four read replicas to spread the read load.
cards.why: Auto Discovery is not in use, so only endpoint config changes; moving to Redis means rewriting code against Redis APIs.

cards.scenario: Legacy single-instance queue app; improve availability, durability, latency; clients time out at 10 seconds; minimize cost.
cards.ok: API Gateway service proxy puts items in SQS; smaller EC2 Auto Scaling group scales on approximate number of queue messages.
cards.bad: API Gateway REST API with Lambda proxy integration; migrate the processing code into a Lambda function behind it.
cards.why: Lambda proxy is synchronous, and processing takes 90 seconds against API Gateway's 29-second limit and the 10-second client timeout; SQS stores messages durably.

cards.scenario: Migrate Redis leaderboard database; durable, microsecond reads, no server management, MOST durable storage.
cards.ok: Amazon MemoryDB cluster with Multi-AZ read replica, seeded from a Redis snapshot in S3; migrate application servers with MGN.
cards.bad: ElastiCache (Redis OSS) with a Multi-AZ replication group, seeded from a Redis snapshot in S3; migrate application servers with MGN.
cards.why: MemoryDB stores writes durably in a Multi-AZ transaction log; ElastiCache can lose data. MGN cannot migrate a database into MemoryDB.

cards.scenario: Transfer Family SFTP files transformed every 5 minutes, then queue message; LEAST operational overhead.
cards.ok: Transfer Family on S3, EventBridge rule triggers Glue ETL on upload, second EventBridge rule sends SQS message on job completion.
cards.bad: Transfer Family on EFS with Glue job scheduled every 5 minutes; Glue must be coded to send SQS messages.
cards.why: Event-driven S3 upload trigger beats scheduled polling; EFS needs file system access management and Glue-to-SQS needs custom code.

cards.scenario: Migrate PHP order system using ActiveMQ proprietary protocol and a JSON document database; LEAST migration effort.
cards.ok: Rehost on EC2 Auto Scaling with ALB; move to DynamoDB for JSON documents; replatform the queue to Amazon MQ.
cards.bad: Replatform the queue to Amazon SQS, or refactor the document database into relational Amazon RDS.
cards.why: SQS supports only HTTP/HTTPS, not ActiveMQ protocol; Amazon MQ is managed ActiveMQ; JSON suits DynamoDB better than relational.

cards.scenario: SQS standard queue causes duplicates and no scaling; fix duplicates and scaling delay, MOST scalable.
cards.ok: Create a new SQS FIFO queue with deduplication; scale on a custom backlog-per-instance metric with target tracking.
cards.bad: Convert the existing standard queue to FIFO; scale on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric.
cards.why: A standard queue cannot be converted to FIFO; visible-message count does not track fleet size, so use backlog per instance.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB on-demand with midnight loads, bursty reads on few repeated keys; cut cost, LEAST overhead.
cards.ok: Deploy DAX for repeated key reads; use provisioned capacity mode with DynamoDB auto scaling.
cards.bad: Deploy DAX and auto scaling and purchase Savings Plans in Cost Explorer on the table.
cards.why: Auto scaling does not work with on-demand mode, and Savings Plans do not apply to DynamoDB; DAX caches hot keys.

cards.scenario: EC2 behind ALB with RDS Multi-AZ; slow repeated reads, CPU spikes; native automated Multi-AZ failover.
cards.ok: ElastiCache for Redis OSS to cache database reads, plus an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones as ALB target.
cards.bad: ElastiCache for Memcached to cache database reads, plus two more manually registered EC2 instances with the ALB.
cards.why: Memcached lacks native automatic Multi-AZ failover, and manually added instances give no self-healing; Redis and Auto Scaling do.

cards.scenario: S3 Standard data, mixed access in first 6 months, rarely accessed after 180 days, retrievable within 6 hours.
cards.ok: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Archive Access tier activated and 180 days until transition (retrieval 3-5 hours).
cards.bad: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier activated and 180 days until transition (retrieval 12 hours).
cards.why: Deep Archive Access retrieval takes about 12 hours, missing the 6-hour limit; Archive Access takes 3-5 hours and handles unknown access patterns.

cards.scenario: Migrate legacy physical Windows app with custom OS settings and IBM Db2, 90 days, prefer managed services.
cards.ok: Rehost the Windows server to EC2 with AWS Transform MGN; migrate Db2 to RDS for MySQL with DMS and SCT replication agent.
cards.bad: Rehost the Db2 Linux VM to EC2 with MGN, and migrate the Windows server to EC2 with DataSync.
cards.why: Custom OS settings make MGN rehost the only option for the app; managed RDS suits the database. DataSync cannot migrate servers or databases.

cards.scenario: Migrate 150 VMs with minimal downtime and 300 TB; internet transfer takes 5 days; FASTEST.
cards.ok: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration for the data (about 5 days) and AWS Transform MGN for the VMs.
cards.bad: Use Snowball devices for the data (about 7 days) and AWS Transform MGN for the VMs.
cards.why: Snowball needs about 7 days versus about 5 for Transfer Acceleration; MGN adds live incremental replication, unlike VM Import/Export.

cards.scenario: IoT data kept forever; frequent access first 6 months, known pattern afterwards; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: S3 Lifecycle rule on the existing bucket to move all data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 180 days.
cards.bad: Create an S3 Intelligent-Tiering configuration on the existing bucket with automatic archiving starting at 180 days.
cards.why: Access patterns are known and unchanging, so Lifecycle is cheaper; Intelligent-Tiering is for unknown patterns and is slow to move data into cheaper tiers.

cards.scenario: Pilot-light backup Region, RTO under 15 minutes, automatic failover, budget excludes active-active.
cards.ok: Route 53 failover routing with health check; unhealthy status alarms via SNS to Lambda that promotes the replica and scales the ASG.
cards.bad: Latency-based Route 53 routing between both ALBs, with a CloudWatch 5XX alarm invoking Lambda to promote the replica and scale the ASG.
cards.why: Latency routing would send traffic to the inactive backup site (ASG min and max zero); failover routing sends traffic there only after failure.

cards.scenario: Back up S3, EBS, EFS, RDS and Storage Gateway volumes with Regional protection; LEAST operational overhead.
cards.ok: AWS Backup vault in another Region and a cross-Region backup plan covering S3, EBS, EFS, RDS, and Storage Gateway volumes.
cards.bad: Create an RDS cross-Region read replica and use a cross-Region AWS Backup plan for the remaining services.
cards.why: AWS Backup covers every listed service in one plan; read replicas are not backups and add unnecessary operational overhead.

cards.scenario: Highly customized, interdependent legacy C++ apps; highly available and scalable; LEAST migration effort.
cards.ok: Use AWS Transform MGN to rehost the applications on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.
cards.bad: Containerize the applications and deploy the Docker images on Amazon ECS using the EC2 launch type.
cards.why: Rehosting keeps the fine-tuned servers unchanged; containerizing customized operating systems and apps needs significant effort.

cards.scenario: Two copies of the app share files across servers; need highly available application and files.
cards.ok: Second EC2 instance in another Availability Zone, both sharing an EFS Standard file system.
cards.bad: Second EC2 instance in another Availability Zone, sharing the files through EBS Multi-Attach.
cards.why: EBS Multi-Attach works only within a single AZ and gives no high availability for data; EFS is multi-AZ and shared.

cards.scenario: Second-Region EC2 repeatedly reads small, rarely changing S3 data; cut data-transfer cost, MOST cost-effectively.
cards.ok: Create a second-Region S3 bucket with gateway endpoint and replicate with S3 Cross-Region Replication.
cards.bad: Interface endpoint via PrivateLink plus VPC peering so second-Region instances read the original bucket.
cards.why: Gateway endpoints are free and CRR charges transfer only on rare changes; repeated reads then cost no cross-Region transfer.

cards.scenario: Aurora global database across two Regions; read-after-write consistency and regular DR tests; LEAST overhead.
cards.ok: Use secondary endpoint for reads and writes with write forwarding; test DR with managed planned failover.
cards.bad: Secondary endpoint for reads, primary endpoint for writes; test DR with managed planned failover.
cards.why: Secondary reads can be stale without write forwarding, so read-after-write fails; managed planned failover automates demotion and promotion.

cards.scenario: Multi-Region DR must handle full load FASTEST; second-Region ALB and Auto Scaling group already exist.
cards.ok: Cross-Region RDS read replica promoted when needed, with Route 53 failover routing policy.
cards.bad: Cross-Region RDS read replica promoted when needed, with Route 53 weighted routing policy.
cards.why: Failover routing shifts traffic automatically; weighted routing needs manual intervention. Restoring from backups is slower than promoting a replica.

cards.scenario: PostgreSQL DR from us-east-1 to us-west-2 with 30-second RPO; minimum application change.
cards.ok: Aurora PostgreSQL global database, primary us-east-1 and secondary us-west-2, with managed RPO set to 30 seconds.
cards.bad: RDS for PostgreSQL with a us-west-2 read replica and managed RPO set to 30 seconds.
cards.why: Managed RPO is a feature of Aurora global databases, not RDS; DynamoDB would need major application changes.

cards.scenario: Static files stay on premises 6 months while apps move to S3; single copy; multiple servers need access.
cards.ok: S3 File Gateway connected to the bucket, with an on-premises NFS file share for the directory.
cards.bad: Volume Gateway connected to the bucket, with an on-premises iSCSI volume for the directory.
cards.why: NFS is a shared file system for multiple servers; iSCSI volumes cannot be shared across hosts without extra configuration.

cards.scenario: Recreatable transcoded videos: daily access 60 days, infrequent 6 months, rare after; retrieve within 5 hours, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: S3 Standard 60 days, S3 One Zone-IA for 6 months, then S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
cards.bad: S3 Standard 60 days, S3 Standard-IA for 6 months, then S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
cards.why: Files can be recreated so One Zone-IA is cheaper; Deep Archive retrieval takes up to 12 hours, exceeding the 5-hour limit.

cards.scenario: Second-Region EC2 needs infrequent, low-volume access to a large S3 dataset without internet; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Interface VPC endpoint for S3 via PrivateLink in the first Region, VPC peering, and access the single bucket.
cards.bad: Second-Region S3 bucket with gateway endpoint, copy existing data and configure Cross-Region Replication.
cards.why: Large stored data with low transfer makes duplicating the dataset costlier than accessing a single bucket across the network.

cards.scenario: No one may delete or overwrite S3 objects for 5 years; existing bucket uses default settings.
cards.ok: Create a new bucket with Versioning and Object Lock, 5-year retention in compliance mode; move existing objects.
cards.bad: Modify the existing bucket to turn on Versioning and Object Lock with 5-year compliance mode retention.
cards.why: Object Lock can be configured only when a bucket is created, so a new bucket is needed; governance mode permits privileged deletion.

cards.scenario: Many accounts and Regions; consolidate GuardDuty, Macie, Access Analyzer findings; LEAST operational overhead.
cards.ok: Use Organizations with Security Hub activated, a designated Security Hub administrator account, and member accounts for consolidated findings.
cards.bad: Activate Security Hub in each account manually, with an administrator account and an aggregation Region, without Organizations.
cards.why: With Organizations, Security Hub auto-detects new accounts; without it each new account needs manual configuration, adding overhead.

cards.scenario: Lambda functions use hardcoded RDS credentials that broke after password change; LEAST development effort.
cards.ok: Store credentials in Secrets Manager, retrieve them from Lambda, and configure single user automatic rotation.
cards.bad: Store credentials in Secrets Manager, retrieve them from Lambda, and configure alternating users automatic rotation.
cards.why: The database has only one shared application user, so the single user strategy fits; alternating users rotation needs two users.

cards.scenario: Millions of unencrypted S3 objects; encrypt all and list sensitive data; LEAST development effort.
cards.ok: Macie finds sensitive data, enable default encryption, then S3 Inventory plus Batch Operations encrypt existing objects in place.
cards.bad: Macie finds sensitive data, but objects move to a new encrypted bucket and all applications are updated.
cards.why: In-place Batch Operations needs no app changes; a new bucket forces code changes and testing. Inspector does not scan S3 for sensitive data.

cards.scenario: S3 prefixes mk, sa, ex with per-role access; add prefixes later; LEAST ongoing administration.
cards.ok: One bucket with S3 access points per prefix group, each with its own policy; share access point aliases.
cards.bad: One bucket with folders; attach resource policies to the folders and give out folder URLs.
cards.why: IAM policies cannot attach to objects or folders; access points give per-group policies and new ones are easy to add.

cards.scenario: Replace internet-facing bastion: stop brute-force SSH, log session commands, keep port forwarding.
cards.ok: Systems Manager Session Manager for administrators, close SSH, terminate the bastion; sessions are logged and support port forwarding.
cards.bad: AWS Client VPN with certificates, security group allows only the Client VPN CIDR, terminate the bastion.
cards.why: Client VPN cannot record commands run during SSH sessions; Run Command cannot forward ports.

cards.scenario: Get timely notice of KMS key deletion requests; LEAST operational effort.
cards.ok: EventBridge rule on KMS key deletion sends an SNS message to the systems administrator, who cancels if needed.
cards.bad: EventBridge rule on KMS key deletion invokes a Lambda function that automatically cancels the deletion request.
cards.why: Administrator must review whether deletion was intentional; automatic cancellation is inappropriate. Athena queries add more effort.

cards.scenario: Enforce SSH only from trusted CIDRs in 50 accounts, non-modifiable by member accounts, via Firewall Manager.
cards.ok: Network Firewall policy with a stateless rule group allowing trusted SSH at the lowest order priority and restricting 0.0.0.0/0.
cards.bad: Network Firewall policy with a stateful strict-order rule group allowing trusted SSH at the highest order priority.
cards.why: Rules evaluate from the lowest number first; the highest-priority allow would be evaluated last, after the deny blocks everything.

cards.scenario: Keys need FIPS 140-2 Level 3, available only 8:00-18:00 Eastern on weekdays; highly available, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Multi-AZ CloudHSM cluster deleted and recreated from backup by scheduled Lambda; metadata in Systems Manager Parameter Store standard parameters.
cards.bad: Keep keys in AWS KMS and schedule Lambda functions to disable and enable the stored keys.
cards.why: KMS is only FIPS 140-2 Level 2; Parameter Store standard parameters are free, whereas DynamoDB for metadata adds cost.

cards.scenario: Multi-account ASG scale-in leaves S3 objects; cleanup within minutes; LEAST operational overhead using EventBridge.
cards.ok: Forward aws.autoscaling events from each account to a central event bus and invoke one central Lambda function to clean up S3.
cards.bad: Create an EventBridge rule in each account and run a separate Lambda cleanup function in every account.
cards.why: One central Lambda means one code base to update; per-account functions duplicate pipelines and code, which makes operations cumbersome.

cards.scenario: Daily EBS backups enforced consistently across Organizations accounts, MOST reliably.
cards.ok: Create an Organizations backup policy that uses AWS Backup and attach it to the organization root.
cards.bad: Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy an AWS Backup plan to every account.
cards.why: Backup policy plans cannot be edited or deleted inside member accounts; StackSets stack instances can be deleted locally, so enforcement is not guaranteed.

cards.scenario: Reliable, durable log of infrastructure changes from SDK and console; must detect alterations to log files.
cards.ok: One CloudTrail trail to a private S3 bucket with log file integrity validation turned on.
cards.bad: One CloudTrail trail to a private S3 bucket with server-side encryption configured on the bucket.
cards.why: Only log file integrity validation can identify altered log files; encryption does not detect changes, and one trail already records SDK and console actions.

cards.scenario: Website scales with demand; sporadic compute-intensive video analysis on fixed on-demand T2 instances; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Website on T2: Reserved for off-peak baseline, On-Demand for peak. Video analysis on a Spot Fleet of C4 and C5 instances.
cards.bad: Website on T2: Spot for off-peak baseline, Reserved for peak. Video analysis on Reserved R4 and R5 in an Auto Scaling group.
cards.why: Reserved suits predictable baseline, On-Demand suits unpredictable peaks, Spot suits sporadic analysis, and compute-optimized C family fits compute-intensive work.

cards.scenario: CFO wants alert at projected 75% EC2 spend and EC2 stopped; LOWEST risk of overspending.
cards.ok: Budget alert on projected costs at 75%, filtered by instance type, with an AWS Budgets action to stop instances.
cards.bad: Budget alert on projected costs at 75%, filtered by instance type, notifying an operator to stop instances manually.
cards.why: Manual stop can be delayed and cause overspending; an automatic Budgets action stops instances immediately. Actual-cost alerts come too late.
